In that encounter seventy-four of our horse were slain; among them, Piso...

This means that Piso was a horse. Yeah, I know there's an obsolete usage of "horse" as "cavalry", but this is stupid. The Latin text even says "equitibus" which would be better rendered as "knight" since it denotes both a military rank and a social rank. But then, I kept reading... Proelio is a combat or struggle, not a tepid "encounter". Piso wasn't so much "descended from a very illustrious family" as "born into the highest rank". There's no "and had been styled" -- Caesar declared that the ancestor was named/called (appellatus) a friend of Rome in a participle.

McDevitte and Bohn published this rubbish translation in 1869. I wish publishers such as Red and Black would throw the ailing classics world a bone and pay for new translations, rather than keep reprinting what should be relegated to Google books...
